method: monotone word-overlap difflib; heuristic, not semantic proof

units.source_text: You might barely have spontaneous words in your mind and still be perfectly capable of thinking a sentence on purpose. Try it and see.
units.output_text: Even if you do n't have any words coming to mind to express what you feel like saying to him, you can still try to think of a sentence to say to him.

units.source_text: If words are there, use them; say the thing aloud, write it, whatever gets it out of the strange imaginary-conversation zone. And if that starts feeling like homework you're doing for a child who isn't answering, drop it.
units.output_text: If you do, use those words to say or write something to him, instead of just talking to him in your imagination.

units.source_text: Maybe what's actually happening is a knot in your stomach, an urge to leave, some image that keeps coming up, a song that suddenly feels relevant. Sometimes nothing “answers” and you just know what would be kind.
units.output_text: But if this feels like homework, skip it-he may be responding in other ways that you can identify (butterflies, urge to run, recurring images, song lyrics, etc.)

units.source_text: The order gets murky too. Feeling can precede language, language can expose a feeling, and afterward you may not know which happened first.
units.output_text: Or you may not get any response at all, and still have a good idea of what would be a loving thing to say to him.

units.source_text: I don't think you need to solve that before using whatever words eventually help you understand it.
units.output_text: It may or may not be possible to tell which came first, the feeling or the words you use to understand the feeling. But that does n't matter-you can still use words to help you understand your feelings.
